title: Rook against two connected pawns
summary: When two pawns beat the rook, how rook and king stop them, and counting the tempi.
part.sixth.title: On the sixth, the pawns win
part.sixth.summary: With no kings nearby, two connected pawns on the sixth rank are stronger than the rook.
part.fifth.title: On the fifth, the move decides
part.fifth.summary: One step earlier, the rook alone still wins, if it is its move and it attacks from the side.
part.king.title: The rook's king counts the squares
part.king.summary: With your king close, the rook wins even against pawns on the sixth. One square farther, and it loses.
part.escort.title: The king escorts the pawns
part.escort.summary: The other side: the king hides from the checks and the right pawn advances.
part.resource.title: Mating threats
part.resource.summary: When the pawns have already arrived, the rook can still draw by threatening the black king on the edge.
part.recap.title: Summary
part.recap.summary: Three rules and the ending in the practical challenge.
step.t_sixth: Black's pawns are already on their sixth rank, and neither king is close. The white rook is to move. Can it stop both?
step.t_sixth.hint1: Try each rook move and see what the other pawn does in reply.
step.t_sixth.hint2: If the rook stands in front of one pawn, the other one moves. If it attacks both, one advances, guarded by the other.
step.sixth: It can't. Each pawn is two steps from promoting, and as soon as one advances, the other guards it. If the rook goes to f1, the g-pawn advances; if it goes to g1, the f-pawn does. If it takes a pawn, the other one is already through. Here every White move loses. The kings on a8 and h8 take no part: it is the rook alone against the two pawns, and at this point the pawns are stronger.
step.d_sixth: Watch the duel from Black's side. The rook tries both files, and the pawns always answer with the other one.
step.d_sixth.m1: 1.Rf1: the rook stands in front of the f-pawn.
step.d_sixth.m2: 1...g2! The other pawn moves. Now it threatens to queen on g1.
step.d_sixth.m3: 2.Rg1: the rook rushes in front of the g-pawn.
step.d_sixth.m4: 2...f2! The pawn attacks the rook on g1 and threatens to queen on f1.
step.d_sixth.m6: ...and the other one queens. Queen against rook, and Black wins.
step.euwe: Max Euwe, a world champion, taught a rule of thumb: two connected pawns on the sixth are worth a rook. In this position you can see the count: added together, the squares the two pawns still need are only four. Even with Black to move, the rook can't hold. Notice it is the reverse of what you just saw: here the pawns are White's and the rook is Black's. The rule works both ways.
step.push: Now you play the pawns. The rook has attacked both along the third rank. Don't waste time with the king: push.
step.push.hint: 1...f2 or 1...g2: the pawn that moves is guarded by the other one. Then the other pawn runs too.
step.push.done: A new queen. The rook was late to every square: with the pawns on the sixth, each of their moves is a threat, and the rook can only answer one.
step.t_fifth: Now the pawns are one step back, on the fifth. The kings are still far away, and the rook is to move. Is there a winning move?
step.t_fifth.hint1: In the last position the pawns needed only two steps. Here they need three. The rook has one tempo to spare.
step.t_fifth.hint2: Look for a square from which the rook attacks both pawns at once.
step.fifth: 1.Ra4! The rook goes to the pawns' rank and attacks both from the side. The g-pawn is stuck: if it advances, the rook takes the f-pawn and the g-pawn is left alone. If the f-pawn advances, the g-pawn falls. And if Black does nothing, the rook takes on f4. Either way one pawn is left alone, and a lone pawn the rook catches from behind. It is the only move: anything else draws or loses.
step.fifthTempo: The same position, but Black is to move. Now a pawn reaches the sixth before the rook gets organised: after 1...f3, the rook can win only one of the pawns, and the other, with the black king helping, is enough for a draw. On the fifth rank, whoever has the move decides. That is why this ending is counted, not guessed.
step.fifthMove: Your turn: attack the pawns from the side and collect what is left.
step.fifthMove.hint: 1.Ra4, on the pawns' rank. After 1...Kg7, 2.Rxf4. After 2...g3, the rook goes back to the g-file.
step.fifthMove.done: One pawn has fallen and the rook has the other under control. Now just bring the king and finish it off.
step.t_king: The pawns are back on the sixth, but now your king is on c4, not on a8. The rook alone was losing. And with the king nearby?
step.t_king.hint1: Count how many moves your king needs to stand next to the squares the pawns will pass.
step.t_king.hint2: The pawns need two moves to reach the first rank. The rook on a1 already watches that whole rank.
step.king: With the king close, the rook wins. It stays where it is, guarding the first rank, and the king runs diagonally: 1.Kd3 and then 2.Ke2 or 2.Ke3, next to the pawns. Together, king and rook do what the rook alone couldn't: the king guards the promotion squares the rook doesn't cover and attacks the pawns up close. Fine and Benko sum it up: with the rook's king far away, two pawns win; with it close, the rook wins.
step.kingLate: Now the same position with the king one square to the side, on b4. It looks like nothing, but it is one more move to e2, and the pawns don't wait: after 1.Kc3 f2, both pawns arrive before the king. It loses. In this ending you count square by square, as in the king's race against a pawn.
step.d_king: Watch the king arrive in time. Notice the rook doesn't move: it is already doing its job on a1.
step.d_king.m1: 1.Kd3: diagonally, towards the squares in front of the pawns.
step.d_king.m2: 1...g2: the pawn threatens g1, but the rook covers that square.
step.d_king.m3: 2.Ke3! The king attacks f3 and watches f2. The pawns are frozen.
step.d_king.m4: 2...Kg7: the black king tries to come, but it is too far away.
step.d_king.m7: 4.Kxg2: the second pawn. King and rook against king: the rest is technique.
step.kingMove: Now your king is on c3. Count the squares and arrive in time.
step.kingMove.hint: 1.Kd2: always towards e2. After 1...f2, 2.Ke2, and then the rook attacks the g-pawn.
step.kingMove.done: Just in time. The king holds f1 and the f-pawn, and the rook takes care of the rest. Note that 1.Kc2 or 1.Kb3 lost: only the moves that bring the king closer to the pawns win.
step.t_escort: Switch sides: now you have the pawns, with your king close, and the black king is far away. The black rook will give checks. What is the way to promote?
step.t_escort.hint1: If you push g6 at once, see which check the rook gives and what it gains.
step.t_escort.hint2: Look for a square for the king where the rook can't reach it with checks, and only then push.
step.escort: Haste ruins everything. If 1.g6, 1...Rh5+! and the rook gains the time it needed: a draw. The king first needs shelter: on h7, in front of the h-pawn, the rook can't check along the h-file, and the g-pawn is free to run. It is the king that escorts the pawns, not the other way round.
step.d_escort: Watch the king go to its shelter before the pawns move.
step.d_escort.m1: 1.Kg6! The king protects both pawns and heads for h7.
step.d_escort.m2: 1...Kc7: the black king runs, but it is too far.
step.d_escort.m3: 2.Kh7: the shelter. The rook has no check, because the h-pawn blocks the file.
step.d_escort.m7: 4.g7, and g8 comes next. The rook would have to give itself up for the pawn.
step.escortMove: The same on the other side of the board. Shelter the king, and only then push.
step.escortMove.hint: 1.Kb6, then 2.Ka7, in front of the a-pawn. Only then 3.b6.
step.escortMove.done: The king on a7 blocks the a-file and guards b8. The black rook has no checks, and the b-pawn walks all the way.
step.t_resource: Black already has the pawns on the sixth and their king is close to the edge. The rook alone can't stop the pawns. Is there a way out?
step.t_resource.hint1: Look at the black king, not at the pawns. Where is it, and where is your king?
step.t_resource.hint2: A check on the g-file, with your king nearby, pushes the black king to the edge.
step.resource: The pawns can't be stopped any more. But the black king is right next to the h-file, and your king is very close to it. 1.Rc1! prepares 2.Rg1+, and after 2...Kh4 your king goes to f4: now the threat is 4.Rh1, mate. The black king has to flee the threats instead of helping the pawns, and White repeats the threats until the draw.
step.d_resource: Watch how the white rook and king make Black go round in circles.
step.d_resource.m1: 1.Rc1! The rook goes to the first rank, on its way to g1.
step.d_resource.m3: 2.Rg1+: the black king goes to the edge.
step.d_resource.m5: 3.Kf4! Now 4.Rh1 would be mate. The black king has no time for the pawns.
step.d_resource.m7: 4.Kf3! The same threat, one rank lower.
step.d_resource.m8: 4...Kh4: the king comes back, and White repeats. A draw.
step.resourceTrap: Watch the trap on the other side: if at the end the black king goes to h2 instead of h4, it escapes the threats, but it also abandons the pawns. 1.Ra1! and the rook goes back to them: it takes a2, then b2. The black king must stay close to your king for the draw to hold.
step.resourceMove: The rook is now on c7. Find the way out and hold the draw.
step.resourceMove.hint: 1.Rc1, on the way to the g-file. After 1...a2, 2.Rg1+. After 2...Kh4, 3.Kf4.
step.resourceMove.done: A draw. The rook didn't stop the pawns; the mating threats took Black's time away.
step.recap: Three rules for your games. First: two connected pawns on the sixth, with no kings nearby, beat the rook. Before that, on the fifth, the rook that has the move attacks both from the side and wins.
step.rules: Second: the rook's king changes everything, but it must arrive in time, and that is counted square by square, diagonally. Third: on the pawns' side, the king hides from the checks before the pawn moves; on the rook's side, when the pawns are already through, look for mating threats.
step.recapMove: One last time, on the other side of the board: the pawns are on the fifth and the rook is to move.
step.recapMove.done: That's it. Attack from the side, and the pawn that is left is alone.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge, in the position with your king on c4. Count the squares, don't let the rook leave the first rank too early, and win.
ex.e06: Black to play and win. From the game Parligras against Gopal, Gibraltar 2012. The pawns are well advanced, and the white rook is behind them. Pawn or king?
ex.e06.hint: With the rook behind the pawns, the king is the one that must help first.
ex.e06.solution: 60...Ka2! The king steps in front of the a-pawn and guards b3 and b2. Now the b-pawn walks with an escort, and the white king arrives too late. That is what Gopal played. If 60...a2 instead, White brings the king in time and it is a draw: a2 is the pawn that no longer needed to move.
ex.e12: White to play and win. Now you have the pawns against the black rook, with your king close and the black one far away. What is the move?
ex.e12.hint: One pawn is alone in front, the other stayed behind. How do they start protecting each other?
ex.e12.solution: 1.h5! The back pawn comes closer and now protects the one on g6. The two walk together, with the king alongside, and the rook can't stop both. The hasty 1.g7 allows 1...Rg1, the rook behind the pawn, and the h-pawn is too far back: a draw. King moves give the rook the time it needed. Position from Mavens's study on Lichess.
ex.e13: White to play and win. The pawns are not both on the sixth yet, but one of them is already there. A check or another move?
ex.e13.hint: The check attacks nothing. Look for a square where the rook attacks a pawn from behind.
ex.e13.solution: 1.Rg6! The rook goes behind the g-pawn. After 1...Kd7, 2.Rg4! attacks both, and after 2...g2, 3.Rxg2: the f-pawn is alone and the black king is far away. The check 1.Ra7+ looks natural but only draws; king moves like 1.Ka7 allow 1...f3, both pawns on the sixth, and lose. From Audax6's study on Lichess.
ex.e14: White to play and win. From the game Leko against Markowski, Polanica Zdroj 1998. Now the pawns are split. The h-pawn is right there to be taken. Do you take it?
ex.e14.hint: The h-pawn isn't going anywhere: the rook watches it along the h-file. Which pawn is really running, and who can catch it?
ex.e14.solution: 66.Kf2!! The king first. The h-pawn is held by the rook and the king, and the danger is the c-pawn. After 66...Kd2, 67.Rxh2 (or 67.Kf1): now the rook takes with your king one step away, and the discovered 68.Kf1+ wins the missing tempo. The greedy 66.Rxh2? loses that tempo: 66...c3, 67...c2 and 68...Kd2, and the c-pawn with its king alongside is worth a draw. Leko played 66.Kf2.
ex.e16: White to play and win. From the game Nabaty against Zelcic, Malinska 2014. The pawns are on the fifth and the black king stands right in front of yours. Which way does your king come back?
ex.e16.hint: Through the front, the black king bars the way. The pawns don't protect the squares behind them.
ex.e16.solution: Kf7! The king goes around the pawns from behind, along the g-file. After g4, Kg6 (or Rc1), and the king reaches the pawns where the black king can't get in the way. Checks don't help: the game went Rc5+, and with Kf4! the black king would have barred the white one and drawn. Kf7 is the only winning move.
ex.e15: Black to play and draw. From the game Shankland against Gao, Doha 2014. Your two pawns can't reach the first rank before the white king comes back. How do you hold?
ex.e15.hint: You don't need both pawns: one costing the rook is enough. Before pushing, look at the white king's path.
ex.e15.solution: 40...Ke5! Your king stands in the white king's path, shouldering it away. After 41.Kc5, 41...h4; after 42.Kc4, 42...Ke4, always in the way. When the rook gets behind one pawn (43.Rh7), push the other: 43...g5. The rook takes one pawn, the other costs the rook, and it is a draw. Every move was the only one. Pushing 40...h4 right away loses: 41.Kd5! and the white king gets back in time. That is how Gao held against Shankland.
ex.e17: White to play and draw. A study by Ladislav Prokeš, 1939. The black pawns are on the sixth, with their king next to them, and your king is far away. There are four only moves to the draw.
ex.e17.hint: The rook alone can't hold. The king has to reach the pawns, and the rook can buy it time, even by giving itself up.
ex.e17.solution: 1.Kg4! The king comes first; checks right away lose. After 1...e2, 2.Rc1+! (to 2...Kd4) and 3.Kf3! The king attacks e2. After 3...d2, 4.Rc4+!! The rook gives itself up: 4...Kxc4 and 5.Kxe2. The white king stands in front of the d-pawn and the draw is safe. Notice that no white move had an alternative: this is Prokeš's manoeuvre.
ex.e18: White to play and win. A study by Richard Réti. Now there are three pawns on the second rank, but your king is right among them. Which pawn first?
ex.e18.hint: Taking a pawn at once looks obvious, but watch the tempo. One king square holds two pawns at the same time.
ex.e18.solution: 1.Kf2! The king watches e1 and g1 at once. After 1...Ke4, 2.Kxe2: two split pawns are left. Now the rook attacks the g-pawn along the g-file (3.Rg1; 3.Ra1, 3.Re1 and 3.Kd2 also win), and after 3...Ke4, 4.Re1 (or 4.Ra1, 4.Rc1): the black king can't stay close to both pawns. 1.Kxg2? allows 1...Ke4, the e-pawn goes with tempo and the black king reaches the c-pawn: a draw; 1.Rxc2? loses.
key.sixth: Two connected pawns on the sixth rank with both kings far away: the rook alone cannot hold. Any White move loses.
key.fifth: One rank earlier, the rook still wins, but only if it is its move and it attacks the pawns from the side. With Black to move, it is a draw.
key.king: The rook's king counts too: here it is close enough and the rook wins. One square further away, and the pawns get through.
key.euwe: Euwe's rule: two connected pawns on the sixth rank are worth a rook. Black is to move and cannot stop them.
key.escort: The king walks with the pawns and hides from the checks in front of them; only then does the right pawn advance.
key.resource: The pawns are almost there, but the rook still draws: instead of chasing them, it threatens to mate the black king.
history: Two connected pawns, side by side, can be stronger than a rook: once they get close to promoting, each protects the other and the rook alone cannot cope. This ending has no famous discoverer, but it has practical rules that are passed from book to book. World champion Max Euwe and Walter Meiden wrote that two connected pawns on the sixth rank are worth a rook; Reuben Fine and Pal Benko added that it all depends on where the rook's king is. The count is tight, and often a single move changes the result. The ending turns up in grandmaster games too, such as Shankland against Maghsoodloo in Prague, 2022, where the king escorted the pawns all the way.
practice: Now the practical challenge: rook against two pawns on the sixth, with your king close. Count the squares and win.
